source_text: Post haec et pro peccatis nostris precamur dicentes: et remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. post subsidium cibi petitur et uenia delicti, ut qui a Deo pascitur in Deo uiuat nec tantum praesenti et temporali uitae sed aeternae consulatur, ad quam ueniri potest, si peccata donentur quae debita Dominus appellat, sicut in euangelio suo dicit: dimisi tibi omne debitum, quia me rogasti. quam necessario autem, quam prouidenter et salubriter admonemur quod peccatores sumus qui pro peccatis rogare conpellimur, ut dum indulgentia de Deo petitur, conscientiae suae animus recordetur! ne quis sibi quasi innocens placeat et se extollendo plus pereat, instruitur et docetur peccare se cottidie, dum cottidie pro peccatis iubetur orare. sic denique et Iohannes in epistula sua monet dicens: si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus et ueritas in nobis non est. si autem confessi fuerimus peccata nostra, fidelis et iustus est Dominus qui nobis peccata dimittat. in epistula sua utrumque conplexus est, quod et rogare pro peccatis debeamus et inpetremus indulgentiam cum rogamus. ideo et fidelem dixit Dominum ad dimittenda peccata fidem pollicitationis suae reseruantem, quia qui orare nos pro debitis et peccatis docuit paternam misericordiam promisit et ueniam secuturam.
thought_title: Forgiveness of debts as daily confession
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the petition 'forgive us our debts' from the Lord's Prayer, after treating the petition for daily bread.
pass_a_gloss: After these things we also pray for our sins, saying: and forgive us our debts, just as we also forgive our debtors. After the support of food, pardon of sin is also sought, so that the one who is fed by God may live in God, and not only may provision be made for the present and temporal life but for the eternal life, to which one can come if sins are forgiven, which the Lord calls debts, just as he says in his gospel: I forgave you all the debt, because you asked me. But how necessarily, how providently and healthfully we are admonished that we are sinners, we who are compelled to ask for sins, so that while pardon is sought from God, the mind may remember its own conscience! Lest anyone please himself as if innocent and by exalting himself perish the more, he is instructed and taught that he sins daily, while daily he is commanded to pray for sins. So finally John also warns in his epistle, saying: if we say that we do not have sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. But if we have confessed our sins, the Lord is faithful and just, who may forgive us sins. In his epistle he has embraced both things, that we both ought to ask for sins and that we obtain pardon when we ask. Therefore he also called the Lord faithful, keeping the faith of his promise for forgiving sins, because he who taught us to pray for debts and sins promised fatherly mercy and that pardon would follow.

choices.why: The glossary gives 'debts' for debita, understood as sins owed to God; keeping the financial metaphor preserves the Lord's Prayer wording.
uenia is pardon or forgiveness, and delictum is sin; the singular 'sin' keeps the abstract sense of the source.
consulo here means to take care for or provide for; the passive impersonal sense fits the context of caring for eternal life.
fidelis means faithful, keeping promises; this rendering preserves the covenant nuance of God's promise to forgive.
rejected: he said the Lord is trustworthy

choices.why: paternam is fatherly, tying back to the opening address 'our Father'; misericordia is mercy, not just kindness.

pass_b_english: After this we pray also for our sins, saying: and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors (Matthew 6:12). After the provision of food, pardon of sin is asked for, so that the one who is fed by God may live in God, and provision may be made not only for this present and temporary life but for eternal life. We can come to that life if our sins are forgiven—the sins the Lord calls debts, as he says in his Gospel: I forgave you all that debt because you asked me (Matthew 18:32). How necessary, how provident and salutary, is the reminder that we are sinners, since we are compelled to pray for our sins! While pardon is being sought from God, the mind recalls its own conscience. So that no one may please himself as if he were innocent and perish by exalting himself, he is instructed and taught that he sins daily, since he is commanded daily to pray for his sins. This is what John also urges in his letter when he says: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, the Lord is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:8-9). In his letter he joined both things together: that we ought to pray for our sins, and that we obtain pardon when we pray. Therefore he called the Lord faithful, because he keeps faith with his promise to forgive sins; for the one who taught us to pray for our debts and sins promised fatherly mercy and the pardon that would follow.

problems.quote: the mind is made to remember its own conscience
problems.why: 'recordetur' is middle/deponent (recalls/remembers), not passive ('is made to remember'). The mind itself remembers its own conscience; no external agency makes it remember.
problems.fix: the mind recalls its own conscience

edits.old: the mind is made to remember its own conscience
edits.new: the mind recalls its own conscience

fixed: Changed 'the mind is made to remember its own conscience' to 'the mind recalls its own conscience': source 'conscientiae suae animus recordetur' has 'recordetur' as deponent/middle ('recalls'), not passive ('is made to remember').

problems.why: 'fidem...reseruantem' means 'keeping faith with his promise,' not 'the faith of his promise.'
problems.ruling: 'fidem pollicitationis suae reseruantem' means 'keeping faith with his promise,' not 'the faith of his promise.' Meaning changed.

edits.old: because he keeps the faith of his promise to forgive sins
edits.new: because he keeps faith with his promise to forgive sins

fixed: Changed 'the faith of his promise' to 'keeps faith with his promise' to match 'fidem pollicitationis suae reseruantem'.

last_rejected.quote: Therefore he called the Lord faithful
last_rejected.why: Subject is John, not 'he'; John called the Lord faithful in 1 John 1:9.
last_rejected.fix: Therefore John called the Lord faithful
last_rejected.ruling: Subject is 'he' referring back to John; 'ideo et fidelem dixit Dominum' has no explicit subject, so 'he' is correct anaphoric reference.
